### A.5 Beta functions

Now that we have evaluated the self-energies and the vertex corrections we can obtain the renormalization factors defined in Eq. (117). We choose the external frequency such that $-i\nu+\lambda=\mu$ and demand the cancellation of poles in the expressions for the renormalized vertices and Green’s functions. Consequently we obtain,

$$ \displaystyle Z_{f} \displaystyle=1-\frac{g_{1}^{2}}{2\bar{r}}-\frac{g_{2}^{2}}{2\bar{r}}-\frac{3\gamma^{2}}{4\epsilon}\,, \displaystyle Z_{b} \displaystyle=1-\frac{g_{1}^{2}}{\bar{r}}-\frac{v^{2}}{\epsilon^{\prime}}\,, \displaystyle Z_{d} \displaystyle=1-\frac{g_{2}^{2}}{\bar{r}}-\frac{v^{2}}{\epsilon^{\prime}}\,, \displaystyle Z_{g_{1}} \displaystyle=1-\frac{g_{2}^{2}}{2\bar{r}}\,, \displaystyle Z_{g_{2}} \displaystyle=1-\frac{g_{1}^{2}}{2\bar{r}}\,, \displaystyle Z_{\gamma} \displaystyle=1+\frac{\gamma^{2}}{4\epsilon}\,, \displaystyle Z_{v} \displaystyle=1\,. $$

Using the expressions for vertex renormalizations in Eq. (117) and Eqs. (128) - (134) we find the beta functions,

$$ \displaystyle\beta(g_{1}) \displaystyle\equiv\mu\frac{dg_{1}}{d\mu}=-\bar{r}g_{1}+\frac{1}{2}g_{1}^{3}+\frac{1}{2}g_{1}g_{2}^{2}+\frac{3}{8}g_{1}\gamma^{2}+\frac{g_{1}v^{2}}{2}\,, \displaystyle\beta(g_{2}) \displaystyle\equiv\mu\frac{dg_{2}}{d\mu}=-\bar{r}g_{2}+\frac{1}{2}g_{1}^{2}g_{2}+\frac{1}{2}g_{2}^{3}+\frac{3}{8}g_{2}\gamma^{2}+\frac{g_{2}v^{2}}{2}\,, \displaystyle\beta(\gamma) \displaystyle\equiv\mu\frac{d\gamma}{d\mu}=-\frac{\epsilon}{2}\gamma+\gamma^{3}+g_{1}^{2}\gamma+g_{2}^{2}\gamma\,, \displaystyle\beta(v) \displaystyle\equiv\mu\frac{dv}{d\mu}=-\frac{\epsilon^{\prime}}{2}v+v^{3}+g_{1}^{2}v+g_{2}^{2}v\,. $$

Note that the vertex corresponding to the fermionic bath is $g$ and so $g_{1}=g_{2}=g$ . Therefore we have,

$$ \displaystyle\beta(g) \displaystyle=-\bar{r}g+g^{3}+\frac{3}{8}g\gamma^{2}+\frac{gv^{2}}{2}\,, \displaystyle\beta(\gamma) \displaystyle=-\frac{\epsilon}{2}\gamma+\gamma^{3}+2g^{2}\gamma\,, \displaystyle\beta(v) \displaystyle=-\frac{\epsilon^{\prime}}{2}v+v^{3}+2g^{2}v\,. $$

These are identical to the beta functions obtained in Sec. III where we used the electron operator instead of the fractionalized operators. The discussion of the fixed points is therefore same as in Sec. III.3.

### A.6 Stability of fixed points

Here we discuss the stability of the fixed points (Eqs. (24)-(31)) by looking at the eigenvalues of the following stability matrix:

$$ J\equiv\begin{bmatrix}J_{1}&J_{2}&J_{3}\\
J_{4}&J_{5}&J_{6}\\
J_{7}&J_{8}&J_{9}\end{bmatrix}\,, $$

where,

$$ \displaystyle J_{1} \displaystyle\equiv\frac{\partial\beta(g)}{\partial g}=-\bar{r}+3g^{2}+\frac{3}{8}\gamma^{2}+\frac{v^{2}}{2}\,,~~~~J_{2}\equiv\frac{\partial\beta(g)}{\partial\gamma}=\frac{3}{4}g\gamma\,,~~~~J_{3}\equiv\frac{\partial\beta(g)}{\partial v}=gv\,, \displaystyle J_{4} \displaystyle\equiv\frac{\partial\beta(\gamma)}{\partial g}=4\gamma g\,,~~~~J_{5}\equiv\frac{\partial\beta(\gamma)}{\partial\gamma}=-\frac{\epsilon}{2}+3\gamma^{2}+2g^{2}\,,~~~~J_{6}\equiv\frac{\partial\beta(\gamma)}{\partial v}=0\,, \displaystyle J_{7} \displaystyle\equiv\frac{\partial\beta(v)}{\partial g}=4vg\,,~~~~J_{8}\equiv\frac{\partial\beta(v)}{\partial\gamma}=0\,,~~~~J_{9}\equiv\frac{\partial\beta(v)}{\partial v}=-\frac{\epsilon^{\prime}}{2}+3v^{2}+2g^{2}\,. $$

We shall consider $\bar{r}>0$ , $\epsilon>0$ and $\epsilon^{\prime}>0$ . From the eigenvalues,

$$ E^{(1)}_{1}=-\bar{r}\,,~~~E^{(1)}_{2}=-\frac{\epsilon}{2}\,,~~~E^{(2)}_{3}=-\frac{\epsilon^{\prime}}{2}\,, $$

it is immediately clear that the Gaussian fixed point $FP_{1}$ is unstable. The fixed point $FP_{2}$ has the following eigenvalues:

$$ E^{(2)}_{1}=2\bar{r}\,,~~~E^{(2)}_{2}=\frac{4\bar{r}-\epsilon}{2}\,,~~~E^{(2)}_{3}=\frac{4\bar{r}-\epsilon^{\prime}}{2}\,. $$

So $FP_{2}$ is stable for any $\epsilon<4\bar{r}$ and $\epsilon^{\prime}<4\bar{r}$ . The fixed point $FP_{3}$ is unstable and has one relevant direction as seen from the eigenvalues,

$$ E^{(3)}_{1}=\epsilon\,,~~~E^{(3)}_{2}=\frac{3\epsilon-16\bar{r}}{2}\,,~~~E^{(3)}_{3}=-\frac{\epsilon^{\prime}}{2}\,. $$

$FP_{4}$ is stable if $4\bar{r}<\epsilon<16\bar{r}/3$ and $\epsilon^{\prime}<16\bar{r}-3\epsilon$ , which follows from its eigenvalues,

$$ E^{(4)}_{1}=5\epsilon-16\bar{r}-\Psi\,,~~~E^{(4)}_{2}=5\epsilon-16\bar{r}+\Psi\,,~~~E^{(4)}_{3}=\frac{16\bar{r}-3\epsilon-\epsilon^{\prime}}{2}\,, $$

where $\Psi=\sqrt{768\bar{r}^{2}-384\bar{r}\epsilon+49\epsilon^{2}}>0$ . The fixed point $FP_{5}$ is unstable and has one relevant direction as is evident from the eigenvalues,

$$ E^{(5)}_{1}=-\frac{\epsilon}{2}\,,~~~E^{(5)}_{2}=\epsilon^{\prime}\,,~~~E^{(5)}_{3}=\frac{\epsilon^{\prime}-4\bar{r}}{4}\,. $$

The fixed point $FP_{6}$ has the eigenvalues,

$$ E^{(6)}_{1}=\epsilon\,,~~~E^{(6)}_{2}=\epsilon^{\prime}\,,~~~E^{(6)}_{3}=\frac{-16\bar{r}+3\epsilon+4\epsilon^{\prime}}{16}\,. $$

Thus it is stable if $-16\bar{r}+3\epsilon+4\epsilon^{\prime}>0$ . We will discuss the eigenvalues at $FP_{7}$ ,

$$ E^{(7)}_{1}=\frac{4\bar{g}^{2}-\epsilon}{2}\,,~~~E^{(7)}_{2}=0\,,~~~E^{(7)}_{3}=16\bar{r}-8\bar{g}^{2}\,. $$

It is then clear that $FP_{7}$ is marginally stable if $2\bar{r}>\bar{g}^{2}>\epsilon/4$ . The first inequality is trivially satisfied by the points on the ellipse describing $FP_{7}$ . The second inequality is satisfied if $\epsilon<4\bar{r}$ (since $\bar{g}^{2}<\bar{r}$ ), which leads to atleast one stable fixed points. For lower values of $\epsilon$ there is a fixed line on the ellipse describing $FP_{7}$ .

The stability of $FP_{8}$ can be best studied by looking at the characteristic equation,

$$ E^{3}+AE^{2}+BE+C=0\,, $$

where $A=-J_{1}-J_{5}-J_{9}=-2(g^{*2}+\gamma^{*2}+v^{*2})<0$ , $B=J_{1}J_{5}+J_{1}J_{9}+J_{5}J_{9}-J_{2}J_{4}-J_{3}J_{7}=g^{*2}\gamma^{*2}+4\gamma^{*2}v^{*2}>0$ , and $C=J_{3}J_{7}J_{5}+J_{2}J_{4}J_{9}-J_{1}J_{5}J_{9}=6g^{*2}\gamma^{*2}v^{*2}>0$ , with $g^{*},\gamma^{*},v^{*}$ being the values at $FP_{8}$ . It is clear that $C=-E^{(8)}_{1}E^{(8)}_{2}E^{(8)}_{3}$ , $B=E^{(8)}_{1}E^{(8)}_{2}+E^{(8)}_{1}E^{(8)}_{3}+E^{(8)}_{2}E^{(8)}_{3}$ , and $A=-(E^{(8)}_{1}+E^{(8)}_{2}+E^{(8)}_{3})$ , where $E^{(8)}_{i}$ are the eigenvalues. So, if $FP_{8}$ is real, one of its eigenvalue is negative and so it is an unstable fixed point.

### A.7 Anomalous dimensions of spinon, holon and doublon operators

We will now evaluate the anomalous dimensions of the fractionalized particles $f$ , $b$ , and $d$ . Although, we must keep in mind that these are not gauge-invariant operators and these exponents are not physical observables. In terms of the renormalization factors, the anomalous dimensions are,

$$ \eta_{f}=\left.\mu\frac{d\ln Z_{f}}{d\mu}\right|_{FP}\,,~~~~~\eta_{b}=\left.\mu\frac{d\ln Z_{b}}{d\mu}\right|_{FP}\,,~~~~~\eta_{d}=\left.\mu\frac{d\ln Z_{d}}{d\mu}\right|_{FP}\,. $$

In terms of the coupling constants,

$$ \displaystyle\eta_{f} \displaystyle=2g^{2}+\frac{3}{4}\gamma^{2}\,, \displaystyle\eta_{b} \displaystyle=2g^{2}+v^{2}\,, \displaystyle\eta_{d} \displaystyle=2g^{2}+v^{2}\,. $$

At the fixed points, we obtain,

$$ \displaystyle FP_{1}:\eta_{f}=0\,,~~~~\eta_{b}=0\,,~~~~\eta_{d}=0\,, \displaystyle FP_{2}:\eta_{f}=2\bar{r}\,,~~~~\eta_{b}=2\bar{r}\,,~~~~\eta_{d}=2\bar{r}\,, \displaystyle FP_{3}:\eta_{f}=\frac{3\epsilon}{8}\,,~~~~\eta_{b}=0\,,~~~~\eta_{d}=0\,, \displaystyle FP_{4}:\eta_{f}=2\bar{r}\,,~~~~\eta_{b}=8\bar{r}-\frac{3\epsilon}{2}\,,~~~~\eta_{d}=8\bar{r}-\frac{3\epsilon}{2}\,, \displaystyle FP_{5}:\eta_{f}=0\,,~~~~\eta_{b}=\frac{\epsilon^{\prime}}{2}\,,~~~~\eta_{d}=\frac{\epsilon^{\prime}}{2}\,, \displaystyle FP_{6}:\eta_{f}=\frac{3\epsilon}{8}\,,~~~~\eta_{b}=\frac{\epsilon^{\prime}}{2}\,,~~~~\eta_{d}=\frac{\epsilon^{\prime}}{2}\,, \displaystyle FP_{7}:\eta_{f}=2\bar{g}^{2}\,,~~~~\eta_{b}=\frac{\epsilon^{\prime}}{2}\,,~~~~\eta_{d}=\frac{\epsilon^{\prime}}{2}\,, \displaystyle FP_{8}:\eta_{f}=-\frac{2\bar{r}}{3}\,,~~~~\eta_{b}=\frac{\epsilon^{\prime}}{2}\,,~~~~\eta_{d}=\frac{\epsilon^{\prime}}{2}\,. $$

### A.8 Anomalous dimensions of spin, electron and SC order-parameter operators

Now we calculate the anomalous dimensions of the electron, spin, and SC order-parameter operators, which are gauge-invariant. These exponents are physical observables in scattering and spectroscopic experiments. Our aim is to evaluate the exponents corresponding to the spin correlator $\langle\vec{S}(\tau)\cdot\vec{S}(0)\rangle$ , the electron correlator $\langle c_{\alpha}(\tau)c_{\alpha}^{\dagger}(0)\rangle$ , and the SC order-parameter correlator $\langle\Delta(\tau)\Delta^{\dagger}(0)\rangle$ . To proceed, we add a source term corresponding to these operators in the action,

$$ \mathcal{S}_{c}=\frac{1}{\beta}\sum_{i\omega_{n}}\left(\Lambda_{S}f^{\dagger}_{\alpha}\frac{\sigma^{a}_{\alpha\beta}}{2}f_{\beta}+\Lambda_{c}[f^{\dagger}_{\alpha}b+\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}f_{\beta}d^{\dagger}+H.c.]+\Lambda_{\Delta}(\Delta+H.c.)\right)\,. $$

Here we have expressed the spin, electron, and SC order-parameter operators in terms of the fractionalized operators: $\hat{S}=f^{\dagger}_{\alpha}({\sigma^{a}_{\alpha\beta}}/{2})f_{\beta}$ , $c_{\alpha}^{\dagger}=f^{\dagger}_{\alpha}b+\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}f_{\beta}d^{\dagger}$ and $\Delta=d^{\dagger}b$ . In terms of these operators the spin, electron, and SC order-parameter are composite operators. Within the field-theoretic RG scheme, we have

$$ \Lambda_{S}=\frac{Z_{ff}\Lambda_{S,R}}{Z_{f}}\,,~~~~~\Lambda_{c}=\frac{Z_{fb}\Lambda_{c,R}}{\sqrt{Z_{f}Z_{b}}}=\frac{Z_{fd}\Lambda_{c,R}}{\sqrt{Z_{f}Z_{d}}}\,,~~~~~\Lambda_{\Delta}=\frac{Z_{D}}{\sqrt{Z_{b}Z_{d}}}\Lambda_{\Delta R}\,. $$

The composite operators $\hat{S}=f^{\dagger}_{\alpha}({\sigma^{a}_{\alpha\beta}}/{2})f_{\beta}$ , $c_{\alpha}^{\dagger}=f^{\dagger}_{\alpha}b+\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}f_{\beta}d^{\dagger}$ , and $\Delta=d^{\dagger}b$ are renormalized as follows:

$$ \hat{S}=\sqrt{Z_{S}}\hat{S}_{R}\,,~~~~~c=\sqrt{Z_{c}}c_{R}\,,~~~~~\Delta=\sqrt{Z_{\Delta}}\Delta_{R}\,. $$

Just like in Ref. [20], even in this case the diagrams involved in the above vertex corrections are exactly the same as those involved in the vertex corrections of $g$ , $\gamma$ , and $v$ vertices evaluated in Sec. A.4. Note that this is true at all orders in $\epsilon$ , $\bar{r}$ , and $\epsilon^{\prime}$ and not just at one-loop level. Setting $g_{1}=g_{2}=g$ , we thus have,

$$ \displaystyle Z_{S} \displaystyle=\left(\frac{Z_{f}}{Z_{\gamma}}\right)^{2}=1-\frac{2\gamma^{2}}{\epsilon}-\frac{2g^{2}}{\bar{r}}\,, \displaystyle Z_{c} \displaystyle=\frac{Z_{f}Z_{b}}{Z_{g1}^{2}}=\frac{Z_{f}Z_{d}}{Z_{g2}^{2}}=1-\frac{3\gamma^{2}}{4\epsilon}-\frac{g^{2}}{\bar{r}}-\frac{v^{2}}{\epsilon^{\prime}}\,, \displaystyle Z_{\Delta} \displaystyle=\frac{Z_{b}Z_{d}}{Z_{v}^{2}}=1-\frac{2g^{2}}{\bar{r}}-\frac{2v^{2}}{\epsilon^{\prime}}\,. $$

These renormalization factors are exactly the same as evaluated in Sec. III.4. The consequent discussion of anomalous dimension is thus identical to that discussed in Sec. III.4.

### A.9 Density correlator

Next, we shall now evaluate the correlator of the density $n=1+d^{\dagger}d-b^{\dagger}b$ . This quantity has been of recent interest and can be measured in a M-EELS experiment. The strategy to evaluate this quantity is the same as in the last two subsections via introducing a source term with vertex renormalization $Z_{nb}$ in the action. We find that at the one-loop level there are no vertex corrections to the correlator $\langle nb^{\dagger}b\rangle$ to order $g^{2}$ , but there is a one-loop correction to order $v^{2}$ . Hence it is straightforward to see that

$$ Z_{n}=\left(\frac{Z_{b}}{Z_{nb}}\right)^{2}=\left(\frac{Z_{d}}{Z_{nb}}\right)^{2}=1-\frac{2g^{2}}{\bar{r}}-\frac{4v^{2}}{\epsilon^{\prime}}\,. $$

Using this we can obtain the anomalous dimension for the density correlator,

$$ \eta_{n}=\frac{d\ln Z_{n}}{d\ln\mu}=4g^{2}+4v^{2}\,. $$

Note that higher-order corrections in $\epsilon$ , $\epsilon^{\prime}$ and $\bar{r}$ will change the value of this exponent. At the fixed points we have,

$$ \displaystyle FP_{1}:\eta_{n}=0\,, \displaystyle FP_{2}:\eta_{n}=4\bar{r}\,, \displaystyle FP_{3}:\eta_{n}=0\,, \displaystyle FP_{4}:\eta_{n}=16\bar{r}-3\epsilon\,, \displaystyle FP_{5}:\eta_{n}=2\epsilon^{\prime}\,, \displaystyle FP_{6}:\eta_{n}=2\epsilon^{\prime}\,, \displaystyle FP_{7}:\eta_{n}=4\bar{g}^{2}+4\bar{v}^{2}\,, \displaystyle FP_{8}:\eta_{n}=\frac{16\bar{r}}{3}-\epsilon+\frac{2\epsilon^{\prime}}{3}\,. $$

At the fixed points $FP_{6}$ (Eq. (29)) and $FP_{8}$ (Eq. (31)), we have $\eta_{n}=2$ and $\eta_{n}=7/3$ , using the self-consistent values of $\epsilon=\epsilon^{\prime}=1$ and $\epsilon=\epsilon^{\prime}=2\bar{r}=1$ respectively. There will be corrections to these values though.

## Appendix B Solving the saddle point equations in large- $M$ analysis

We proceed by introducing a low-frequency ansatz for the Green’s functions defined earlier. In terms of the imaginary time, $\tau$ , such that $|\tau|\gg 1/J$ we write at $T=0$ ,

$$ \displaystyle G_{a}(\tau)=-\text{sgn}(\tau)\frac{C_{a}\Gamma(2\Delta_{a})\sin(\pi\Delta_{a}+\text{sgn}(\tau)\theta_{a})}{\pi|\tau|^{2\Delta_{a}}}\,, $$

where parameters $C_{a}$ , $\Delta_{a}$ and $\theta_{a}$ are real. To simplify the expression, we define

$$ C_{a}^{\pm}=\frac{C_{a}\Gamma(2\Delta_{a})\sin(\pi\Delta_{a}\pm\text{sgn}(\tau)\theta_{a})}{\pi}\,. $$

Positivity constraints on the spectral densities impose restrictions on asymmetry angles:

$$ -\pi\Delta_{f}<\theta_{f}<\pi\Delta_{f}\,,\quad\pi\Delta_{b}<\theta_{b}<\pi/2\,,\quad\pi\Delta_{d}<\theta_{d}<\pi/2\,. $$

We can now collect the corresponding expressions for self energies at $|\tau|\gg 1/J$ and $T=0$ by plugging (180) into (61)-(63) and obtain,

$$ \displaystyle\Sigma_{b}(\tau) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\displaystyle-\text{sgn}(\tau)t^{2}\bigg(\frac{C_{b}^{+}C_{f}^{+}C_{f}^{-}}{|\tau|^{4\Delta_{f}+2\Delta_{b}}}-\frac{C_{d}^{-}{C_{f}^{+}}^{2}}{|\tau|^{4\Delta_{f}+2\Delta_{d}}}\bigg)+\text{sgn}(\tau)k^{2}L^{2}\frac{C_{b}^{+}C_{d}^{+}C_{d}^{-}}{|\tau|^{2\Delta_{b}+4\Delta_{d}}}\,, \displaystyle\Sigma_{d}(\tau) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\displaystyle-\text{sgn}(\tau)t^{2}\bigg(\frac{C_{d}^{+}C_{f}^{+}C_{f}^{-}}{|\tau|^{4\Delta_{f}+2\Delta_{d}}}-\frac{C_{b}^{-}{C_{f}^{+}}^{2}}{|\tau|^{4\Delta_{f}+2\Delta_{b}}}\bigg)+\text{sgn}(\tau)k^{2}L^{2}\frac{C_{b}^{+}C_{b}^{-}C_{d}^{+}}{|\tau|^{2\Delta_{d}+4\Delta_{b}}}\,, \displaystyle\Sigma_{f}(\tau) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\displaystyle\text{sgn}(\tau)kt^{2}\bigg(\frac{C_{f}^{+}C_{b}^{+}C_{b}^{-}}{|\tau|^{2\Delta_{f}+4\Delta_{b}}}-\frac{2C_{f}^{-}C_{b}^{+}C_{d}^{+}}{|\tau|^{2\Delta_{f}+2\Delta_{b}+2\Delta_{d}}}+\frac{C_{f}^{+}C_{d}^{+}C_{d}^{-}}{|\tau|^{2\Delta_{f}+4\Delta_{d}}}\bigg)-\text{sgn}(\tau)J^{2}\frac{{C_{f}^{+}}^{2}C_{f}^{-}}{|\tau|^{6\Delta_{f}}}\,. $$

Using the spectral representation of the self energies,

### D.5 Beta functions

We are now in a position to write the beta functions for the coupling constants. Using Eq. 224 we find three equations,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\epsilon}{2}\gamma Z_{S}+\left[Z_{S}-\frac{\gamma}{2}\frac{\partial Z_{S}}{\partial\gamma}\right]\beta(\gamma)-\frac{\gamma}{2}\frac{\partial Z_{S}}{\partial g}\beta(g)-\frac{\gamma}{2}\frac{\partial Z_{S}}{\partial v}\beta(v) \displaystyle=0\,, \displaystyle\bar{r}gZ_{c}+\left[Z_{c}-\frac{g}{2}\frac{\partial Z_{c}}{\partial g}\right]\beta(g)-\frac{g}{2}\frac{\partial Z_{c}}{\partial\gamma}\beta(\gamma)-\frac{g}{2}\frac{\partial Z_{c}}{\partial v}\beta(v) \displaystyle=0\,, \displaystyle\frac{\epsilon^{\prime}}{2}vZ_{\Delta}+\left[Z_{\Delta}-\frac{v}{2}\frac{\partial Z_{\Delta}}{\partial v}\right]\beta(v)-\frac{v}{2}\frac{\partial Z_{\Delta}}{\partial g}\beta(g)-\frac{v}{2}\frac{\partial Z_{\Delta}}{\partial\gamma}\beta(\gamma) \displaystyle=0\,. $$

We have used the exact relations $\widetilde{Z}_{g}=\widetilde{Z}_{\gamma}=\widetilde{Z}_{v}=1$ in obtaining these equations. Solving these three equations and using the expressions for the renormalization factors found above we obtain the following one-loop beta functions,

$$ \displaystyle\beta(g) \displaystyle=-\bar{r}g+\frac{P_{g}}{2}g^{3}+\frac{P_{\gamma}}{2}g\gamma^{2}+\frac{P_{v}}{2}gv^{2}=-\bar{r}g+g^{3}+\frac{3}{8}g\gamma^{2}+\frac{gv^{2}}{2}\,, \displaystyle\beta(\gamma) \displaystyle=-\frac{\epsilon}{2}\gamma+\frac{L_{\gamma}}{2}\gamma^{3}+\frac{L_{g}}{2}\gamma g^{2}+\frac{L_{v}}{2}\gamma v^{2}=-\frac{\epsilon}{2}\gamma+\gamma^{3}+2\gamma g^{2}\,, \displaystyle\beta(v) \displaystyle=-\frac{\epsilon^{\prime}}{2}v+\frac{R_{v}}{2}v^{3}+\frac{R_{g}}{2}vg^{2}+\frac{R_{\gamma}}{2}v\gamma^{2}=-\frac{\epsilon^{\prime}}{2}v+v^{3}+2vg^{2}\,. $$

These are exactly the same as Eqs. (21) - (23) derived in Sec. III.3 using diagrammatic RG with electron operator, as well as Eqs. (139) - (141) found using the fractionalized RG method in Sec. A.5. Therefore the fixed points are also the same as obtained earlier as well as all the exponents. Hence we do not discuss them here again.
